feedback: If a learner describes circuits or wires, redirect: at this stage we only need 'charge builds up, then jumps as a spark'.
Confirm the key link: the spark we see is the lightning; the sound it makes is the thunder — one event, not two.
activities.intendedInsight: Lightning is an electrical discharge — charge builds and then jumps as a spark — and thunder is the sound that spark makes; this is kept qualitative with no circuit detail.
learnerActions: Look at a storm-cloud diagram and identify where charge builds up, where the spark jumps, and where the boom comes from.
Explain in a sentence that charge builds in the cloud and then jumps as a spark (the lightning), and the sound of that spark is the thunder.
activities.title: Name the parts of a storm cloud (supporting scaffold)

feedback: If a learner fears the thunder itself, reassure: thunder is only a sound and cannot hurt you — it is the lightning to respect.
If a learner thinks louder thunder means more dangerous lightning, clarify that loudness mostly tells you the storm is close.
activities.intendedInsight: Loudness of thunder mainly reflects how close the lightning is, not how dangerous the sound is. If you can hear thunder at all, lightning is close enough to be a danger, so go indoors. The gap tells you roughly how far away the storm is and whether it is coming closer, and it is the lightning, not the sound, that poses the danger.
learnerActions: Decide, from whether the flash-to-boom gap is shrinking or growing, whether a storm is coming closer or moving away, and remember that if you can hear thunder at all you should already be indoors, whatever the gap.
Discuss what actually makes the thunder sound, and explain why thunder itself cannot hurt you while lightning is the thing to respect.
Talk through age-appropriate storm-safety rules (e.g. when thunder roars, go indoors, even if the flash-to-boom gap is long).
activities.title: Storm safety and facing the fear
